name: Closed Guard Sweeps
description: Break opponent's posture, create momentum, and sweep them from closed guard using hip bump, scissor, flower, or pendulum mechanics.
shortInstruction: Break posture, off-balance, pull the angle, and sweep — every sweep starts with a broken opponent.
summary: Closed guard sweeps transform your guard from a neutral position into a scoring position. The key principle is that you cannot sweep a well-based opponent — you must first break their posture, off-balance them, and attack when they are reacting. The big four sweeps are the hip bump (forward), scissor (sideways), flower (diagonal), and pendulum (circular). Each one exploits a different reaction to your posture control.
whyItWorks: A broken-postured opponent has their weight loaded forward — this makes them vulnerable to being redirected.
The sweeps work as a dilemma: defend the hip bump, get scissored; defend the scissor, get hip bumped.
Legs are stronger than arms — using your legs to sweep leverages your strongest muscles against their base.
Danaher principle: the sweep is the end product of posture break + angle + momentum.
commonMistakes: Sweeping without breaking posture first — a postured opponent can simply step out of the sweep.
Letting the opponent post on your head during the sweep — frame immediately to prevent this.
Giving up the closed guard after a failed sweep — always have a re-guard plan.
Using only arms to sweep instead of engaging hips and legs.
coachingCues: Break posture before every sweep — no exceptions.
Legs sweep, arms guide — your arms control the direction, your legs provide the power.
Commit fully or don't sweep — halfway sweeps give them the pass.
Sweep to a pin, not just to escape — end on top in control.
safetySummary: Do not crank your partner's neck when pulling them into the sweep — control the body, not the head.
When landing on top after a sweep, protect your own head from hitting the mat.
If they land on your legs during a failed sweep, immediately recover guard to avoid knee pressure.
keyCorrections: Hip bump failed? They posted their arm — switch to a scissor sweep on that same side.
Scissor sweep failed? They stepped over your leg — transition to a triangle or pendulum sweep.
All sweeps failing? Your posture break is weak — go back to posture control first.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Break posture → off-balance → choose sweep based on their reaction → land in a dominant pin.

decisionTree.condition: they defend the sweep by posturing, attack the triangle or armbar instead
decisionTree.action: the guard is a system, not isolated moves.

moneyDetails: For the hip bump, pull their head to your chest and bump with your hips — don't just push with your arms.
For the scissor, cut your bottom leg across their belly while your top leg blocks their shoulder — it's a knee line cut, not a leg push.
For the flower sweep, kick your foot from their hip across their centerline — the momentum comes from the hip, not the foot.
Always end the sweep in a dominant pin (mount, side control, or knee-on-belly) — don't just dump them and reset.
nextStep: After mastering closed guard sweeps, learn the submissions from closed guard (triangle, armbar) to chain with your sweeps.
fixItFast: Hip bump not working? You're pushing, not hip bumping — drive your hips up, not your arms.
Scissor sweep feels weak? Your bottom leg isn't cutting deep enough — bring it higher across their belly.
They keep posting? Use their post as an entry to armbar or kimura.
